summary: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings. Systematic errors spoil accuracy and are not removed by repeating.
Leading zeros never count as significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point do. Sums keep the fewest decimal places, products the fewest significant figures.
Percentage errors always add, each multiplied by its power: %(A^pB^q/C^r) = p%A + q%B + r%C.
Every term in a correct equation has the same dimensions; dimensions convert units and derive power-law relations, but cannot give numerical constants or tell work from torque.
R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2ABcosθ; |A - B| ≤ R ≤ A + B; two equal vectors at 120° have a resultant equal to either.
vec A·vec B = ABcosθ (zero when perpendicular), |vec A×vec B| = ABsinθ (zero when parallel, equals the parallelogram area).
v = u + at, s = ut + (1)/(2)at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, sn = u + (a)/(2)(2n-1); slope of v–t = acceleration, area = displacement.
Projectile: T = 2usinθ/g, H = u^2sin^2θ/2g, R = u^2sin2θ/g; maximum range at 45°; complementary angles give equal ranges.

summary: Inertia is resistance to change of motion, measured by mass; vec F = dvec p/dt; action and reaction are equal, opposite and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.
A weighing machine reads m(g ± a) according to the direction of the acceleration; zero in free fall, mg at constant velocity.
Equilibrium of a rigid body needs zero net force and zero net torque; three concurrent forces in equilibrium obey Lami's theorem.
Impulse = change in momentum = area under the force–time graph; spreading the same impulse over more time lowers the force.
With no external force, total momentum is conserved: recoil, explosions, rockets and every collision.
W = Fscosθ; the net work equals the change in kinetic energy; K = p^2/2m; P = Fv.
Elastic collisions conserve KE (e = 1); perfectly inelastic ones stick together (e = 0) and lose the most KE; equal masses in an elastic head-on collision exchange velocities.
Limiting friction μsN is independent of area of contact; μk < μs; angle of repose = angle of friction, μs = tanθr.
terms: Principle of conservation of linear momentum

units.title: Rotational Dynamics
topics: Moment of inertia of a uniform rod and radius of gyration
Torque, rotational work, kinetic energy and power

sections.title: Moment of inertia of a uniform rod and radius of gyration
Torque, rotational work, kinetic energy and power
Angular momentum and its conservation

summary: Moment of inertia I = Σ mr^2 depends on the mass, its distribution and the axis — not on the angular velocity; it is the rotational analogue of mass.
Uniform rod: ML^2/12 about the centre, ML^2/3 about an end; the centre gives the least I of all parallel axes (I = Icm + Md^2).
Radius of gyration k = √I/M: L/(2√3) about the centre and L/√3 about an end; k doubles when I quadruples.
Torque τ = rFsinθ (unit N m, never joule) and τ = Iα; a force through the axis gives no torque; a couple turns without translating.
Rotational work τθ, power τω, kinetic energy (1)/(2)Iω^2; rotational equations of motion mirror the linear ones.
Angular momentum L = Iω = mvrsinθ (J s); τ = dL/dt.
With zero external torque Iω is constant: the skater, the diver, planets moving faster near the Sun; K = L^2/2I rises when I falls.

units.title: Fluid Statics and Dynamics
topics: Pressure in a fluid; surface tension, surface energy and capillary action

sections.title: Pressure in a fluid; surface tension, surface energy and capillary action

summary: Pressure in a liquid is P0 + hρ g, the same at one level, independent of the vessel's shape; Pascal's law multiplies force in a hydraulic lift; upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced.
Surface tension (N m⁻¹) equals surface energy per unit area (J m⁻²); it falls with temperature and with soap or detergent; a soap film has two surfaces.
Excess pressure is 2T/r in a drop and 4T/r in a soap bubble — the smaller the bubble, the higher the pressure.
Capillary rise h = 2Tcosθ/(rρ g): liquids that wet glass (acute angle, concave meniscus) rise; mercury (obtuse, convex) is depressed; a short tube never overflows.
Viscous force F = η A dv/dx; viscosity of liquids falls and of gases rises on heating; SI unit Pa s.
Stokes' drag 6πη rv leads to the terminal velocity 2r^2(ρ - σ)g/9η, proportional to r^2.
Poiseuille's flow Q = π Pr^4/8η l depends on the fourth power of the radius.
Continuity A1v1 = A2v2 and Bernoulli P + (1)/(2)ρ v^2 + ρ gh = constant: faster flow means lower pressure — venturimeter, Torricelli's √2gh, wing lift, atomisers.

Simple pendulum and spring–mass system; forced oscillation and resonance

summary: In uniform circular motion speed is constant but velocity is not; the acceleration v^2/r = ω^2r points to the centre, and the centripetal force does no work.
The centripetal force is supplied by a real force: friction on a level road (vmax = √μ rg), the normal reaction on a banked road (tanθ = v^2/rg), tension, gravity.
In a vertical circle on a string the least speeds are √gr at the top and √5gr at the bottom; the tension is greatest at the bottom, by 6mg more than at the top.
SHM: acceleration = -ω^2× displacement; x = Asin(ω t + φ), v = ω√A^2 - x^2; speed is greatest at the mean position, acceleration at the extremes.
Total energy (1)/(2)mω^2A^2 is constant; KE = PE at x = A/√2; each form of energy oscillates at twice the frequency.
Simple pendulum T = 2π√l/g (independent of mass, depends on g); spring T = 2π√m/k (depends on mass, independent of g).
Springs in series are softer, in parallel stiffer; half a spring is twice as stiff.
Forced oscillations take the driver's frequency; at resonance (driving frequency = natural frequency) the amplitude is greatest, more sharply so with less damping.

units.title: Gravitation
topics: Newton's law of gravitation; acceleration due to gravity and its variation
Gravitational field strength, potential and potential energy

sections.title: Newton's law of gravitation; acceleration due to gravity and its variation
Gravitational field strength, potential and potential energy
Satellites: orbital velocity, period, energy, escape velocity, geostationary orbit

summary: Every mass attracts every other with F = Gm1m2/r^2; the force is always attractive, mutual, central and conservative.
Surface gravity is g = GM/R^2; it belongs to the planet, not to the falling body.
With height gh = g(R/(R+h))^2 (inverse square); with depth gd = g(1-d/R) (linear, because the outer shell pulls equally all round). g is zero at the centre.
Rotation reduces g most at the equator: gλ = g - Rω^2cos^2λ; the poles have the largest g and the equator the smallest.
Field strength GM/r^2 is a vector in N kg⁻¹; potential -GM/r is a scalar in J kg⁻¹, zero at infinity and negative everywhere else.
Potential energy is -GMm/r; mgh is only its near-surface approximation. The work by an external agent is +Δ U.
Orbital speed √GM/r and period 2π√r^3/GM: higher orbits are slower, and T^2 ∝ r^3.
Satellite energy: K = GMm/2r, U = -GMm/r, E = -GMm/2r. The total is negative and equals -K; raising the orbit increases E but decreases K.

topics: Stress, strain and Hooke's law

sections.title: Stress, strain and Hooke's law
Young's modulus, bulk modulus and modulus of rigidity; Poisson's ratio
Elastic potential energy and energy density

summary: Elasticity is the recovery of shape after a deforming force is removed; beyond the elastic limit the deformation is plastic and permanent.
Stress is force per unit area inside the material (Pa); strain is a fractional change of length, volume or angle and has no unit.
Hooke's law — stress proportional to strain — holds only up to the proportional limit; the constant is the modulus of elasticity.
Y=(FL)/(AΔ L) applies to stretching and compressing solids. It depends on the material, not on the wire's dimensions; the extension itself obeys Δ L∝ L/d^2.
K=-(Δ P)/(Δ V/V) applies to every state of matter; for a gas it is P isothermally and γ P adiabatically.
G=(F/A)/(θ) applies to solids only; liquids and gases have no rigidity.
Poisson's ratio σ=-(Δ d/d)/(Δ L/L) is dimensionless, 0 for cork, about 0.3 for steel and 0.5 for rubber.
The three moduli are linked: Y=2G(1+σ) and Y=3K(1-2σ).

units.title: Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer
topics: Thermal energy, heat and temperature; thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law
Thermometers: liquid-in-glass, resistance and radiation thermometers — principle, advantages and limitations

sections.title: Thermal energy, heat and temperature; thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law
Thermometers
Conduction, convection and radiation; black-body radiation and the Stefan–Boltzmann law

summary: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules; thermal energy is the total internal energy (so it depends on mass); heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference.
Two bodies in thermal contact reach the same temperature — thermal equilibrium — with no net heat flow. The zeroth law makes "same temperature" transitive and so makes thermometry possible.
T=θC+273 and θF=(9)/(5)θC+32; the scales agree at −40°; absolute zero is −273.15 °C.
Liquid-in-glass thermometers read the apparent expansion of the liquid; mercury covers −39 to 357 °C, alcohol −115 to 78 °C.

Resistance thermometers use R=R0(1+αθ) and are the most accurate over a wide range; thermocouples use the Seebeck emf and are small, fast and wide-ranging; pyrometers measure radiation without contact.
Conduction obeys H=kAΔθ/L; the temperature gradient is steepest in the poorer conductor, and thermal resistances L/kA add in series.
Convection is heat carried by a moving fluid; it needs gravity for the natural case.
Newton's law of cooling gives an exponential approach to the surroundings' temperature, with equal fractions of the excess lost in equal times.

units.title: Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat
topics: Linear, superficial and cubical expansion and their relation
Real and apparent expansion of liquids
Heat capacity, specific heat capacity and the method of mixtures
Latent heat of fusion and vaporization; the triple point

sections.title: Linear, superficial and cubical expansion and their relation
Real and apparent expansion of liquids
Heat capacity, specific heat capacity and the method of mixtures
Latent heat of fusion and vaporization; the triple point

summary: Δ L = LαΔ T, Δ A = AβΔ T, Δ V = VγΔ T, with β = 2α and γ = 3α for an isotropic solid. Area takes 2α, volume takes 3α — never the other way round.
A hole or a cavity in a heated plate grows by the same fraction as the metal itself; nothing shrinks on heating except water below 4 °C.
A clamped rod develops σ = YαΔ T, compressive on heating. A pendulum clock runs slow when hot, losing (1)/(2)αΔθ of its time.
A liquid's real expansion exceeds its apparent expansion by the vessel's: γr = γa + γv. The level in a warmed vessel first dips (the glass grows first) and then rises.
Water is densest at 4 °C; that is why ice floats, ponds freeze from the top, and pipes burst in a hard frost.
Q = mcΔ T raises temperature; Q = mL changes phase at constant temperature. Never use both for the same stage.
The calorimeter's water equivalent W = mccc/cw must be added to the water mass. Ignoring it makes the hot body's specific heat come out too low.
In an ice problem, first compare the heat available with mLf. If the ice cannot all melt, the final temperature is 0 °C with ice left over.
terms: Heat capacity and specific heat capacity

units.title: Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics
topics: Ideal-gas equation; kinetic theory: pressure, rms speed and energy of molecules
First law of thermodynamics: isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric and isobaric processes; molar heat capacities
Second law of thermodynamics: internal-combustion engines, refrigerators and entropy

sections.title: Ideal-gas equation; kinetic theory: pressure, rms speed and energy of molecules
First law of thermodynamics: isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric and isobaric processes; molar heat capacities
Second law of thermodynamics: internal-combustion engines, refrigerators and entropy

summary: PV = nRT = NkT; R = NAk; P = ρ RT/M. Temperature must be in kelvin, and one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP.
Kinetic theory gives P = (1)/(3)ρ crms^2, hence crms = √3RT/M: at the same temperature the lighter gas is faster, and doubling crms needs four times the absolute temperature.
Average translational kinetic energy is (3)/(2)kT per molecule whatever the gas; the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on T.
Degrees of freedom 3, 5, 6 give Cv = (f)/(2)R, Cp = Cv + R and γ = 1.67, 1.40, 1.33. Cp > Cv because the extra heat at constant pressure does work.
First law: Q = Δ U + W with W done by the gas; Δ U = nCvΔ T in every process.

Isothermal: Δ U = 0, Q = W = nRTln(V2/V1). Adiabatic: Q = 0, W = -Δ U, PV^γ constant, and the curve is γ times steeper. Isochoric: W = 0, all the heat goes to internal energy. Isobaric: W = nRΔ T, Q = nCpΔ T.
A cycle has Δ U = 0, so Qnet = Wnet = the area enclosed.
η = 1 - Q2/Q1 ≤ 1 - T2/T1, with kelvin temperatures; a real engine is always below the Carnot value.

sections.title: Progressive waves and the wave equation

Stationary waves: harmonics and overtones in strings and pipes
Pressure amplitude, intensity and loudness, pitch and quality
Doppler effect

summary: A progressive wave is y = Asin(ω t - kx), with v = ω/k = fλ; the minus sign means it travels towards +x.
Particle velocity is vp = -vtimesslope of the profile, with maximum Aω — a completely different number from the wave speed.

Sound speed is set by stiffness and density: √Y/ρ in solids, √B/ρ in liquids, √γ P/ρ = √γ RT/M in gases. It rises with temperature, falls with molar mass, and does not change with pressure at constant temperature.

A string fixed at both ends and an open pipe give every harmonic, fn = nv/2L; a closed pipe gives odd harmonics only, fn = (2n-1)v/4L, and has half the fundamental of the open pipe of the same length.
End correction e = 0.3d per open end; the resonance tube removes it by using l2 - l1 = λ/2.
Beats: fb = |f1 - f2|, audible only for small differences; waxing a fork lowers its frequency, filing raises it.
Intensity is 2π^2ρ vf^2A^2, falls as 1/r^2, and converts to loudness by L = 10log(I/I0); +10 dB is ten times the intensity, +3 dB is two sources.
Doppler: f' = f(v ± vo)/(v mp vs) with the upper sign for approach; a source moving away lowers the pitch, and motion across the line of sight gives no shift.

topics: Reflection at curved mirrors: mirror formula and magnification
Refraction at plane surfaces, critical angle and total internal reflection; refraction through a prism

sections.title: Reflection at curved mirrors: mirror formula and magnification
Refraction at plane surfaces, critical angle and TIR; refraction through a prism
Lenses: lens formula, lens maker's formula, power and combinations
Dispersion, chromatic aberration and achromatism

summary: The Cartesian convention fixes everything: origin at the pole or optical centre, positive along the incident light; a real object has u<0, a concave mirror f<0, a convex lens f>0.
Mirror: (1)/(v)+(1)/(u)=(1)/(f) and m=-(v)/(u); R = 2f; a convex mirror is always virtual, erect and diminished.
Refraction: μ = c/v and μ1sin i = μ2sin r; frequency is unchanged at a boundary, wavelength and speed are not.
Apparent depth = d/μ; a slab shifts the ray sideways without changing its direction; sin C = 1/μ, and TIR needs dense-to-rare plus i>C.
Prism: A = r1+r2 and δ = i1+i2-A; at minimum deviation the ray is symmetrical and μ = sin((A+δm)/2)/sin(A/2); a thin prism gives δ = (μ-1)A.
In contact P = P1+P2; separated by d, P = P1+P2-dP1P2. A converging lens in water has a longer focal length — about four times longer for glass.
Dispersion: μ falls as λ rises, so violet bends most; ω measures the spread; a crown–flint doublet with ω1/f1+ω2/f2=0 is achromatic, and mirrors never show chromatic aberration.

units.title: Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction and Polarization
topics: Coherent sources and the conditions for interference; Young's double-slit experiment
Diffraction at a single slit and at a grating; resolving power of optical instruments
Polarization and Brewster's law

sections.title: Coherent sources and the conditions for interference; Young's double-slit experiment
Diffraction at a single slit and at a grating; resolving power of optical instruments
Polarization and Brewster's law

summary: Interference is superposition of coherent waves; intensity is I1+I2+2√I1I2cosφ with φ = 2πΔ/λ. Equal sources give 4I0 bright and zero dark.
Bright fringes need Δ = nλ; dark fringes need Δ = (2n-1)λ/2. Optical path is μ times geometrical path.
Coherent beams are made by dividing a wavefront (double slit) or an amplitude (thin film). Two independent lamps never interfere.
Young's double slit: yn = nλ D/d for bright fringes and β = λ D/d for the spacing — independent of the order, proportional to λ and D, inversely proportional to d, and divided by μ in a liquid.
A slab of thickness t shifts the whole pattern by (μ-1)t/β fringes towards the covered slit without changing β.
In a thin film the reflected beams differ by 2μ tcos r + λ/2; in Newton's rings the reflected centre is dark and rn = √nλ R for dark rings.
Single slit: minima at asinθ = nλ, central maximum of width 2Dλ/a, twice the width of the secondary maxima.
Grating: (a+b)sinθ = nλ; highest order nmax = d/λ; the maxima are sharp because many slits contribute.

topics: Ohm's law and Joule's law; resistance, resistivity, emf, potential difference, energy and power

sections.title: Ohm's law and Joule's law; resistance, resistivity, emf, potential difference, energy and power
Resistors in series and parallel; Kirchhoff's laws
Wheatstone bridge, metre bridge and potentiometer; a galvanometer converted to an ammeter and a voltmeter
Seebeck and Peltier effects; the thermocouple

summary: Current is the rate of flow of charge; I = nAevd with a drift speed of only about 10^-4 m s⁻¹, while the field that drives it travels at nearly light speed.
Ohm's law V = IR holds for metals at constant temperature; R = ρ L/A, and ρ = m/(ne^2τ) is a property of the material, unchanged by cutting or bending.
Metals have α > 0 (about 4×10^-3 K⁻¹), semiconductors α < 0, and alloys such as manganin α ≈ 0, which is why they make standard resistors.
A real cell gives V = E - Ir; the V–I graph has intercept E and slope -r, and the terminal voltage exceeds the emf only while the cell is being charged.
P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R; use I^2R in series and V^2/R in parallel; 1 kWh = 3.6×10^6 J, and the bill is (power in kW) × (hours) × (rate).

Series adds resistances and shares the current; parallel adds conductances and shares the voltage. Cells in series raise the emf, in parallel lower the internal resistance, and mixed rows do both with I = nE/(R + nr/m).
Kirchhoff: charge is conserved at a junction, energy round a loop. Fix a sign convention, solve, and check the power balance.

Wheatstone balance P/Q = R/S; metre bridge R = Sl/(100-l), most accurate with the balance near the middle; potentiometer E ∝ l, a null method that draws no current and so measures emf rather than terminal pd.

units.title: Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties of Materials
topics: Magnetic field of a straight conductor, a circular coil and a long solenoid
Force on a moving charge and on a current-carrying conductor; torque on a coil; Hall effect
Dia-, para- and ferromagnetism: domains, relative permeability, susceptibility and hysteresis

sections.title: Magnetic field of a straight conductor, a circular coil and a long solenoid
Force on a moving charge and on a current-carrying conductor; torque on a coil; Hall effect
Dia-, para- and ferromagnetism: domains, relative permeability, susceptibility and hysteresis

summary: A long straight wire gives B=μ0I/2π r, with circular field lines; two parallel wires with currents in the same direction attract, with F/L=μ0I1I2/2π d.
At the centre of a coil B=μ0NI/2R; on the axis B=μ0NIR^2/2(R^2+x^2)^3/2, which is 0.354 of the centre value at x=R and falls as 1/x^3 far away.
Inside a long solenoid B=μ0nI is uniform, outside it is nearly zero, and at the ends it is half the interior value.

The magnetic force F=qvBsinθ is perpendicular to vec v and does no work, so speed and kinetic energy stay constant; r=mv/qB and T=2π m/qB, independent of speed. A velocity component along vec B turns the circle into a helix of pitch v_∥ T.
A wire feels F=BILsinθ; a coil feels τ=NIABsinθ, maximum when its plane is parallel to the field. A radial field makes a galvanometer's deflection proportional to current.
The Hall voltage VH=BI/net is inversely proportional to thickness, independent of width, and its polarity reveals whether the carriers are positive or negative.

μr=1+chi. Diamagnets have a tiny negative chi and are repelled; paramagnets a tiny positive chi obeying chi=C/T and are attracted; ferromagnets have domains and a very large chi below the Curie point.

The hysteresis loop gives retentivity (residual B), coercivity (field to erase B) and, through its area, the energy lost per cycle. Soft iron's narrow loop suits transformer cores; steel's wide loop suits permanent magnets.

units.title: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Current
topics: Faraday's and Lenz's laws; the AC generator, the transformer and eddy currents
Self and mutual inductance; energy stored in an inductor
Peak and rms values; impedance, phase, power and Q-factor of LCR circuits
Rectification with a diode bridge

sections.title: Faraday's and Lenz's laws; the AC generator, the transformer and eddy currents
Self and mutual inductance; energy stored in an inductor
Peak and rms values; impedance, phase, power and Q-factor of LCR circuits
Rectification with a diode bridge

summary: The flux through a coil is Phi=BAcosθ; the emf is the negative rate of change of flux linkage, varepsilon=-N dPhi/dt, and only a changing flux induces one.
Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change in flux; that opposition is what makes the law a statement of energy conservation.
A rod moving across a field has varepsilon=Bvl; the magnetic drag is B^2l^2v/R and the mechanical power you supply equals the I^2R heat produced.
A coil rotating in a field gives varepsilon=NBAωsinω t; the peak emf is NBAω and it occurs when the flux through the coil is zero.
A transformer obeys Vs/Vp=Ns/Np=Ip/Is; it needs alternating current, cannot change the frequency, and loses energy to copper, eddy currents, hysteresis and leakage.
Self-inductance is NPhi=LI with varepsilon=-L dI/dt; a solenoid has L=μ0N^2A/l, and the stored energy is frac12LI^2, in the field with density B^2/2μ0.
Mutual inductance M couples two coils and is the basis of the transformer; M12=M21.
rms values are peak values divided by √2; the power is VrmsIrmscosφ, never V0I0cosφ.

units.title: Electrostatics and Capacitors
topics: Electric charge, electrostatic induction and Coulomb's law
Electric field of point charges; electric potential and potential energy; Gauss's law
Capacitors: the parallel-plate capacitor, combinations, energy density and the effect of a dielectric

sections.title: Electric charge, electrostatic induction and Coulomb's law
Electric field, potential and Gauss's law
Capacitors

summary: Charge is quantised (q = ne), conserved, and additive as a scalar. One coulomb is 6.25×10^18 electronic charges.
Charging by conduction gives the same sign as the charging body; charging by induction gives the opposite sign, provided the earth is removed before the rod.
Coulomb's law: F = kq1q2/r^2 in vacuum, divided by K in a medium. Forces superpose as vectors, so the net force is found one charge at a time.
The null point of two like charges lies between them, nearer the smaller; for equilibrium of three charges the third is opposite in sign and fixed in magnitude.
Field lines leave positive charge, end on negative charge, never cross, and are perpendicular to conductors. E = 0 inside a conductor, but V is constant there, not zero.
V = kq/r is a scalar; U = qV; E = -dV/dr points downhill in potential.
Gauss's law gives the three standard fields: kQ/r^2 for a sphere, λ/(2πvarepsilon0r) for a line, σ/(2varepsilon0) for a sheet.
C = Q/V = varepsilon0A/d, multiplied by K with a dielectric; series adds reciprocals, parallel adds directly.

units.title: Electrons and Photons
topics: Motion of an electron in electric and magnetic fields
J. J. Thomson's experiment and Millikan's oil-drop experiment
Photons and the photoelectric effect: laws and Einstein's equation

sections.title: Motion of an electron in electric and magnetic fields
J. J. Thomson's experiment and Millikan's oil-drop experiment
Photons and the photoelectric effect: laws and Einstein's equation

summary: An electron in a field along its velocity is accelerated: eV=(1)/(2)mv^2, so v∝√V.
In a transverse electric field the path is a parabola, y=eEx^2/(2mv^2); the oscilloscope deflection VdL^2/(4dVa) does not contain e/m, and it falls when the accelerating voltage rises.
In a magnetic field the path is a circle of radius r=mv/eB, traced at constant speed; the period 2π m/eB is the same for every speed. A velocity component along vec B turns the circle into a helix.

Thomson used crossed fields: balance gives v=E/B, and the radius in the magnetic field alone gives e/m=E/(B^2r)=1.76×10^11 C kg⁻¹. He measured a ratio, and its constancy proved electrons are in all matter.
Millikan held a charged drop stationary, so the drag vanished and qE=mg. Every charge was a whole multiple of e=1.60×10^-19 C: charge is quantised.
A photon has energy hf=hc/λ and momentum h/λ, zero rest mass and no charge. 1240/λ(nm) gives the energy in eV.
The photoelectric laws: a threshold frequency; Kmax set by frequency and metal only; current proportional to intensity; emission instantaneous. The wave theory fails the first, second and fourth.
Einstein: hf=φ+Kmax. Hence f0=φ/h, λ0=hc/φ, and eV0=hf-φ.

summary: Bohr kept the nuclear atom and added stationary states, mvr = nh/2π, and photon emission on a jump, hf = E2 - E1.
For hydrogen rn = 0.529n^2 Å, vn = 2.19×10^6/n m s⁻¹ and En = -13.6/n^2 eV; the ground state is bound by 13.6 eV.
A downward jump n2 → n1 emits 1/λ = R(1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2); each n1 names a series.
Lyman ends on n = 1 and is ultraviolet; Balmer ends on n = 2 and is the only visible series; Paschen, Brackett and Pfund are infrared.
The number of lines from level n is n(n-1)/2; lines crowd to a series limit.
de Broglie: λ = h/p; an electron at 100 V has λ ≈ 1.2 Å, small enough to diffract from crystals, which is the evidence for matter waves.
Δ xΔ p ≥ h/4π: confinement increases momentum spread, which is why electrons cannot live in nuclei and why atomic orbits are not sharp paths.
X-rays come from a Coolidge tube: thermionic electrons accelerated onto a heavy target; over 99 % of the energy becomes heat.

summary: The nucleus has Z protons and A-Z neutrons; R = R0A^1/3, so volume ∝ A and density is the same for all nuclei (2.3×10^17 kg m⁻³).
A nucleus is lighter than its parts by Δ m; the missing mass is the binding energy, Eb = Δ m c^2, with 1 u = 931.5 MeV.
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56 at 8.8 MeV. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move nuclei up this curve and release energy.
Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into two mid-mass fragments plus neutrons, releasing about 200 MeV; a chain reaction needs a critical mass.
Fusion: light nuclei join, releasing energy; it needs about 10^7 K to overcome the Coulomb barrier, and powers the Sun.
Alpha is a helium nucleus (A-4, Z-2), beta is an electron or positron (Z±1), gamma is a photon (no change). Alpha ionises most and penetrates least; gamma is the reverse.
N = N0e^-λ t, T1/2 = 0.693/λ, τ = 1/λ; after n half-lives a fraction 2^-n remains. Half-life is unaffected by temperature or chemical state.
Activity A = λ N, measured in becquerels; 1 Ci = 3.7×10^10 Bq.

sections.title: Energy bands in metals, semiconductors and insulators; intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors
The p–n junction diode, its biasing and its use as a rectifier
Logic gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND and NOR

summary: In a solid the atomic levels broaden into bands; the valence band is full, the conduction band is where moving electrons live, and the gap between them decides the class of the solid.
Metals have no gap (or overlapping bands) and their resistance rises with temperature; semiconductors have Eg of about 1 eV and their resistance falls; insulators have Eg>3 eV.
In an intrinsic semiconductor ne=nh=ni, and conduction is by electron–hole pairs created by thermal energy.
A pentavalent donor makes an n-type crystal (electrons majority); a trivalent acceptor makes a p-type crystal (holes majority). The crystal stays neutral, and nenh=ni^2.
At a p–n junction, diffusion and recombination leave a depletion layer of fixed ions and a barrier of 0.7 V (Si) or 0.3 V (Ge).

Forward bias narrows the depletion layer and lowers the barrier; reverse bias widens it and raises it. The reverse current is a small minority-carrier drift, not zero, and a diode's resistance is not constant.
A diode rectifies: one diode gives half-wave output at f with average 0.318V0; two or four give full-wave output at 2f with average 0.637V0.
AND gives 1 only for 11; OR gives 1 for any 1; NOT inverts; NAND is the negation of AND; NOR the negation of OR.

Nanotechnology
The Big Bang theory and Hubble's law

summary: The Standard Model has six quarks and six leptons, in three generations, each with an antiparticle of the same mass and opposite charge.
Quarks are confined: only combinations are seen. Baryons are three quarks (p=uud, n=udd); mesons are a quark–antiquark pair (π^+=ubar d).

The four interactions are strong (gluon), electromagnetic (photon), weak (W, Z) and gravitational (graviton, not yet observed), with strengths in the approximate ratio 1:10^-2:10^-6:10^-38 and ranges from 10^-18 m to infinity.
The Higgs boson (about 125 GeV/c^2, found at CERN in 2012) is the quantum of the field that gives mass to fundamental particles — not to the photon or gluon, and not most of the mass of a proton.
Nanotechnology works at 1–100 nm, where the surface-to-volume ratio is large and quantum effects set in; real uses include drug delivery, water treatment, coatings and nanoscale transistors.
The Big Bang is supported by the expansion, the 2.725 K CMB and the abundances of the light elements.
Redshift z=Δλ/λ, with v≈ cz for small z; Hubble's law v=H0d with H0≈70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
1/H0≈14 Gyr is a rough age; the accepted age is 13.8 Gyr, and the expansion has no centre.
